analysis.one_liner: Exempts certain large nonbank financial companies from mandatory stress tests.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote in the Senate before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 2008 financial crisis, Congress required the biggest financial companies to run periodic stress tests — simulations showing whether they could survive a severe recession without collapsing. This bill would exempt companies that are not mainly regulated by a federal banking agency or the housing finance regulator, such as large insurers and broker-dealers that answer to the SEC, from that requirement. The SEC and the futures regulator could still order these companies to run stress tests, but only if they choose to. The bill was introduced in late September 2022, sent to the Senate Banking Committee, and never went anywhere before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be large nonbank financial companies — big insurers, broker-dealers, and similar firms whose primary regulator is the SEC or the Commodity Futures Trading Commission rather than a banking regulator. These companies would no longer have to run the periodic stress tests required by the Financial Stability Act of 2010, saving the considerable cost of running and documenting repeated loss simulations. Investors in those companies would benefit from lower compliance expenses. The public would see no direct benefit; the argument for the bill is efficiency, and the countervailing risk is that a weakened early-warning system makes financial failures, which land on ordinary people, somewhat more likely.

how_it_helps.text: The bill exempts financial companies whose main regulator is neither a federal banking agency nor the Federal Housing Finance Agency — for example, insurers and broker-dealers overseen by the SEC — from the statutory requirement to run annual stress tests under the Financial Stability Act of 2010 [S2][S3].
It spares these companies the cost of running repeated hypothetical loss analyses, which the industry has long argued are time-consuming and expensive to perform [S3].

It keeps a backstop: the SEC and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission may still write rules requiring the exempted companies to run stress tests, including checks on liquidity, if those agencies choose to [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall on the financial system's safety net and indirectly on everyone who depends on it. Stress tests are how regulators find out early whether a giant financial firm could collapse in a downturn; weakening that check for nonbanks — the category of firm at the center of the 2008 AIG bailout — raises the chance that a failure is caught late, when the fallout spreads to markets, credit, and potentially taxpayer-supported rescues. The companies themselves save money; the public absorbs the added tail risk.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through added financial-system risk

drawbacks.text: Stress tests are one of the main tools regulators use to catch problems at systemically important nonbank firms before they fail; exempting these firms from the requirement removes a check on large, interconnected companies whose failure could ripple through the financial system and cost ordinary savers and taxpayers.

Even an honest supporter would acknowledge the relief goes to some of the largest financial companies, not small firms — the stress test mandate it lifts applies to big companies, so the compliance savings concentrate at the top of the financial industry.

The bill is not a full exemption: the SEC and CFTC could still write rules requiring the same companies to run stress tests, which means the paperwork burden could return through a different door, making the bill's practical benefit uncertain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is real but narrow: stress tests are expensive, and companies that do not pose the same kind of risk as banks can reasonably argue that a one-size-fits-all mandate wastes money [S2]. The cost is that the companies covered by this bill are large and interconnected, and the 2008 failure of a lightly regulated nonbank insurer showed that a nonbank failure can damage the whole financial system and require taxpayer support [S3]. The bill hedges by letting the SEC and CFTC still impose tests through their own rules, so it is not a full exemption — but it shifts from a standing statutory requirement to a discretionary one, which is a weaker safeguard. On balance, the bill trades a modest, targeted compliance burden for a loss of assured oversight of some of the largest financial firms; the trade favors the firms more than the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced by a Republican senator with one Democratic cosponsor and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 29, 2022, less than four months before the 117th Congress ended [S1][S5].
On the day it was introduced it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs; no further action of any kind appears in the record [S5].
The committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the Senate floor, and the full Senate never voted on it before the Congress adjourned on January 3, 2023 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, large nonbank financial companies did not gain the stress test exemption, and the existing requirement that these companies prove they can absorb losses remained on the books. Ordinary people are no worse off than before it was introduced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public; the stress test rule survived

for.name: Sen. Mike Rounds
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt nonbank financial companies from mandatory stress tests [S1][S3].

for.name: Sen. Jon Tester
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Democratic cosponsor [S3][S4].

for.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
for.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action; the bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor — Sen. Mike Rounds (R-SD) and Sen. Jon Tester (D-MT), the sole Senate Democrat on the bill [S3][S4] — but no faction of either party ever voted on it, so the partisan shape of broader support is unknown.

industries.industry: Nonbank systemically important financial companies (large insurers and other nonbanks overseen by the SEC)
industries.note: These companies would be freed from the statutory stress test requirement, saving the cost of running repeated loss analyses. Their gain comes at the expense of a safety check that protects the broader financial system the public depends on.

industries.industry: Securities broker-dealers and asset managers regulated by the SEC
industries.note: They, too, would be exempt from the automatic stress test mandate, lowering compliance costs. Because they can still be required to test by SEC rule, the relief is partial.

industries.industry: Federal financial regulators (SEC, CFTC, FDIC and other banking agencies)
industries.note: Banking agencies would lose jurisdiction over stress tests for these nonbanks, while the SEC and CFTC gain explicit authority to impose tests by rule. The result is less automatic oversight and more discretion.
